sections.title: Beyond Tradwives: Religion, Family, and the Domestic in North America
sections.description:
In Caro Claire Burke’s 2026 novel Yesteryear, a tradwife influencer who has built her brand around an idealized vision of traditional American domesticity suddenly finds herself confronted with the realities of life in 1855. What happens when fantasies of the “traditional” family collide with the histories they claim to recover? Long before “tradwives” took over social media, religious communities in North America were already creating, practicing, debating, and disrupting different ways of making families, households, and lives together. This course explores these histories from the early colonial period to their contemporary reverberations, asking how religion has shaped—and been shaped by—the everyday practices of marriage, kinship, gender, sexuality, intimacy, home, and belonging.
Drawing on interdisciplinary scholarship, theories, and methods, as well as primary sources and diverse media, we will move from early settler and Indigenous kinship systems to monasticism and polygamy; slavery and the separation and reconstitution of Black families; communal households and queer intimacies; Victorian domestic ideology; and the making of the nuclear family and modern religious visions of family life. Along the way, we will ask: Who gets to count as family? What makes a household respectable, deviant, sacred, or dangerous? How have slavery, racialization, and colonialism shaped whose kinship ties were recognized, protected, disrupted, or denied? How have people made and remade home and belonging under conditions of coercion, displacement, and exclusion? And what role has religion played in all of this?
